22566-dorothy-and-the-wizard-in-oz:
Dorothy and the Wizard in Oz brings two old friends back together. L. Frank Baum's readers had asked for more about the Wizard. Children wrote to him asking what happened to the Wizard afterward.

The Wizard had made hosts of friends in the first Oz book. He frankly acknowledged himself a humbug in that story. Yet children loved him and remembered his balloon ascent. They were all waiting for him to come down again someday. So Baum tells what happened to the Wizard afterward in this volume. Dorothy joins him underground after an earthquake opens the earth. Their adventures run through strange countries beneath the surface. Readers get a favorite pair reunited in Oz's fourth book.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alvarez-caril:
Gil de Albornoz, renowned cardinal, general, and statesman, was born about 1310 at Cuenca in New Castile and died 23 August 1367 at Bonriposo Castle near Viterbo. His father descended from Alfonso V of León, his mother Teresa de Luna from Aragon's royal house. After law at Toulouse he became royal almoner, Archdeacon of Calatrava, and Archbishop of Toledo on 13 May 1338. He accompanied Alfonso XI against the Moors in 1340 and saved the king's life.

Sent to Italy by Innocent VI, he again subjected the whole pontifical territory to papal authority. His successor at Avignon, the Abbot of Cluny, had no military training to face the skilled Ordelaffi, and intrigues complicated the work. He remained only a short time at Avignon before returning to Italy's wars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-badajoz: This 1913 reference article on Badajoz — the Spanish diocese of the Guadiana. Tirso López Bardón gives its story. Its bishops date from antiquity. The Alcazaba crowns the border town. A see of the Extremaduran plain. Its bridge spans the Guadiana's width.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-le-coz: This 1913 reference piece on Claude Le Coz — the Archbishop of Besançon. Joseph Sollier honors his restored rule. He rebuilt the Franche-Comté Church. The entry preserves his modest fame. A prelate of the Concordat's age. His Besançon see was the Jura's own.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hector-berlio: This 1913 reference piece on Berlioz — the French composer. Joseph Otten honors his famous Symphonie. His music fired the romantic age. The world hailed the daring pen. The Shakespeare of the orchestra. His 1869 death is famed.
dorothy-and-the-wizard-in-oz:
L Frank Baum sends Dorothy Gale underground in Dorothy and the Wizard in Oz, the fourth Oz book, subtitled a faithful record of adventures in an underground world. An earthquake drops Dorothy, her cousin Zeb Hugson, the kitten Eureka, and the cab-horse Jim into a crack in the earth. The Wizard of Oz soon falls in beside them, balloon and all.

Their road home runs through a glass city, a vegetable kingdom whose people want to bury them, invisible bears, wooden gargoyles, and dragonettes. Ozma rescues the party with the magic belt, and Eureka stands trial in Oz for eating a piglet. Baum's invention stays generous, and the underground journey gives the series one of its strangest settings.
nasa-tm-19700033121-performance-of-a-10-:
Fred W. Steffen of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in October 1970. It gives the performance of a conical plug nozzle fitted with a stowed thrust reverser. Tests covered flight speeds from a standstill to twice the speed of sound.

Nozzles with two throat areas and two shroud lengths were tested. Steffen compares them with a hinged iris plug nozzle that had no reverser. With its shroud pulled back, the reverser nozzle did better at subsonic cruise, he reports. At other settings the trade went the other way. A stowed reverser lets a jet slow down after landing without harming cruise flight.
the-emerald-city-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum's The Emerald City of Oz brings Dorothy back to Oz for good. Its contents tell the arc in heads: how the Nome King grew angry, how Ozma granted Dorothy's request, and how Dorothy became a princess. The Nome King plots revenge and hires strange allies, from the Whimsies to the Growleywogs, while Dorothy tours odd lands.

Aunt Em and Uncle Henry come to live in Oz at last. Glinda's spell and a drink at the Forbidden Fountain end the threat. Baum meant this as the series' close, and it glows with a fond farewell.
the-lost-princess-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum dedicated The Lost Princess of Oz to his granddaughter Ozma Baum and opened it with a letter to his readers about imagination. Imagination, he argues, carried mankind through the Dark Ages, led Columbus and Franklin to their discoveries, and gave the world the steam engine, telephone, and automobile. A prominent educator, he says, calls fairy tales of untold value in developing that faculty in the young.

Baum then credits the book's main idea to a visitor. A sweet little girl of eleven told him that if Ozma ever got lost or stolen, everybody in Oz would be dreadful sorry. The chapter list begins with A Terrible Loss, the troubles of Glinda the Good, a robbery, and a search party, turning the child's suggestion into an Oz adventure.
the-magic-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum's The Magic of Oz bills itself, in its subtitle, as a record of the adventures of Dorothy, Trot, and the Wizard of Oz. The Cowardly Lion, the Hungry Tiger, and Cap'n Bill join them. Their quest is a magical birthday present for Princess Ozma. The twenty-three chapters promise Mount Munch, conspirators, and the Forest of Gugu. They add an isle of a magic flower, a magic word learned by the Wizard, and a lonesome duck. Ozma's birthday party and the Fountain of Oblivion close the tale.

Baum's letter to his readers begins with a bow to the world. The events of recent years outside, he says, are so marvelous that he despairs of matching them with any tale of Oz. The letter breaks ground for a tale in which the Wizard's magic becomes the prize everyone is chasing.
the-marvelous-land-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum wrote The Marvelous Land of Oz after children flooded him with letters asking for more about the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman. In his author's note, dated from Chicago in June 1904, Baum explains that he promised one young visitor a sequel once a thousand letters arrived. The chapters introduce Tip, who builds a pumpkin-headed man and brings him alive with a magic powder.

Tip's creation, Jack Pumpkinhead, rides a sawhorse that also springs to life. The fugitives flee to the Emerald City, where the Scarecrow now rules as king. General Jinjur leads an army of revolt against him, and the party travels on to seek the Tin Woodman's help. Baum dedicated the book to the two stage actors whose Scarecrow and Tin Woodman had delighted child audiences. Young readers get invention, escape, and a comic revolution in Oz.
the-patchwork-girl-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum wrote The Patchwork Girl of Oz, dedicated to his young friend Sumner Hamilton Britton of Chicago. The prologue explains how more Oz stories came to be written. Baum, as Royal Historian of Oz, had made six books when Ozma's edict cut the land off, invisible to the outside world, and children wrote asking for more.

A child suggested wireless telegraphy. The Historian rigged a tower, learned the art, and called for Princess Dorothy. Glinda the Sorceress, whose great book records every event the moment it happens, would be sure to notice. A Shaggy Man in Oz knew how to reply. The prologue frames the tale as messages from a hidden land.
the-road-to-oz:
L. Frank Baum, royal historian of Oz, sends Dorothy Gale of Kansas onto an enchanted road with the Shaggy Man, Button Bright, and Polychrome the Rainbow's daughter. Contents promise a way to Butterfield, a queer village, King Dox, a city of beasts, a musicker, soup-kettle escapes, a truth pond, and Tik-Tok before the Emerald City and Ozma's birthday.

A letter to readers begins by granting what children asked for: another Oz book. The road structure lets Baum string new countries and creatures between Kansas and the Emerald City. Young readers get a journey built from requests, which keeps its tone obliging and episodic.
the-scarecrow-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum dedicated The Scarecrow of Oz to the uplifters of Los Angeles, California. He thanked them for kindness, consideration, and good-fellowship. A prefatory letter, headed 'Twixt You and Me, follows the dedication. Baum signs it as Royal Historian of Oz.

In that letter, an army of child readers besieged the post office, Baum jokes. Their imperious commands reached him through conquered postmen. They insisted Trot and Cap'n Bill be admitted to the Land of Oz. Trot should enjoy Dorothy, Betsy Bobbin, and Ozma there. The one-legged sailor might befriend the Tin Woodman, the Shaggy Man, and Tik-Tok. Baum says the Scarecrow's best efforts were needed to save the pair. The story leaves them happily in Ozma's palace.
the-wonderful-wizard-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum's The Wonderful Wizard of Oz lists twenty-four chapters in its contents. Dorothy meets the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, and the Cowardly Lion. The party journeys to the Emerald City and the great Oz. Later chapters bring Glinda the Good Witch and the trip home. Baum dedicates the book to his wife, his good friend and comrade.

An introduction begins by placing the tale among folklore and legend. Baum presents Oz as a modern fairy tale for children. Wonder replaces the old tales' moralizing fright. Readers follow a Kansas girl through cyclones and poppy fields. The chapter list alone maps one of America's best-loved fantasy journeys.
tik-tok-of-oz:
L. Frank Baum dedicated Tik-Tok of Oz to composer Louis F. Gottschalk, whose melodies he said breathe fairyland's true spirit. His letter to readers recalls the success of The Patchwork Girl of Oz. Children, he reports, like the Oz stories best of all.

Baum introduces Ann Soforth, Queen of Oogaboo, whom Tik-Tok helped conquer the Nome King, plus Betsy Bobbin reaching Oz. He also promises a future book bringing Trot, Cap'n Bill, Button-Bright, and Ojo together, once Dorothy sends word by wireless. Readers get an Oz adventure introduced as a direct conversation with child readers.
